column12: Children describe how Nigerian militants moving south are seizing more young captives ESINELE, Nigeria (AP) — Aliyu Saheed feared he might not see his three young sons again. For nearly two months after al-Qaida-linked fighters carried out a mass abduction of schoolchildren in an area of Nigeria formerly free of such attacks, he could hardly sleep at night. He wondered what the boys were doing in captivity and how his youngest, just 5 years old, would survive. "The day they told us they had been rescued was the happiest day of my life," the farmer told The Associated Press, as children returned to the community on Friday to feasting and prayers led by pastors and Islamic clerics. His boys were among dozens of students abducted from their classrooms in Oriire area of southwestern Oyo state on May 15 before being rescued on July 10. Children as young as 3 were seized in the attack that awakened many Nigerians to a threat that has been moving south through Africa's most populous nation in the last year. Competition for territory and control of natural resources has intensified among jihadis and other armed groups as they expand beyond the conflict-battered north to areas largely spared until now. Nigeria's forests are used for militants' expansion The armed men stormed into the agrarian community and took 39 children from three schools. They were marched, along with teachers, into a vast forest reserve nearby. One teacher was killed in the abduction. Two others were killed in captivity, according to local media. The forest reserve connects to neighboring Kwara state to the north, which borders northern Nigeria and its long history of mass abductions of students by armed groups, often for ransom. Analysts say children and schools are often seen as strategic targets to draw more attention and higher ransoms. Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has said the attackers in Oyo state were Ansaru militants, a breakaway faction of the Boko Haram militant group that claims to defend the interests of Islam and has been more active in recent years. Authorities said the rescue operation was carried out jointly by the military, intelligence agency and police, and that eight kidnappers were arrested while others were killed. The abduction turned attention to Nigeria's lightly policed forest reserves and their use as a corridor and hiding area for armed groups. "The thing to learn is that the forested areas of the country must be much better surveilled because that is where those armed groups operate and keep their victims," said Joachim MacEbong, a senior analyst at global risk consultancy firm Control Risks. Children described being bound and beaten In interviews with the AP, the children and their parents spoke of horrid conditions in captivity. They said their captors left them in the open without shelter, exposing them to sun and rain. Saheed's eldest son, 9-year-old Shuaib, said he and his brothers tried to distract themselves by thinking about the comfort of home and their mother's cooking. They were fed a basic meal of boiled rice and palm oil, he recalled. "I could not say anything for fear of getting beaten," he said. "They flogged us with a cane all over the body, and they hit me in the back with the butt of their gun." The militants beat the youngest children the worst and muffled their mouths with cloth so that their cries would not attract attention, Alamu Folawe, the head of one of the schools, told journalists. Families said some children now have physical scars, and many are still recuperating psychologically. Aduke Balogun's daughter, 8-year-old Kehinde Kaosarat, was one of the last to be discharged from the hospital. She has not left her mother's side since she returned home on Friday. While in captivity, the girl said, she could not eat or sleep because "I kept imagining the worst things." Abducted siblings Jacob and Mary told their parents after their release that they didn't want to return to school, said their father, Gabriel Sunday. It's a common concern after such kidnappings in a country that already has one of the world's highest numbers of children out of school. "Sending them back to the school does not sound meaningful to me right now," said Saheed, the father of the three boys. The spread to the south increases pressure on leaders Tinubu, elected in 2023 after promising to end the country's security woes, has come under growing pressure. The U.S. military is supporting Nigerian forces, though much of that is restricted to logistics and intelligence-gathering at the heart of the violence in the north. Although Tinubu said the Ansaru militants' network of informants was dismantled during the rescue operation, analysts say the drivers of insecurity, such as corruption and poor governance, remain. And Nigeria's overstretched security forces are mostly absent in remote communities. James Barnett, a research fellow with U.S.-based Hudson Institute who specializes in security in Africa, said Ansaru has been building networks in Nigeria's southwest for many years. Experts say an attack regarded as successful could inspire more. Some residents now hesitate to return Friday's celebration of the children's return drew the community of Christians and Muslims together for dancing and a meal to express their gratitude. "We have all come here to thank God for protecting the children and their teachers and helping the military men who rescued them," said Tajudeen Abioye, the village chief. Many residents left the area after the attack but have started trickling back. Although security forces deployed following the mass abduction are still in the area, locals remain anxious, especially farmers whose farms are close to the forest reserve. "The rescue of the Oriire abductees is wonderful news and should inspire some confidence in Nigeria's ability to better manage these threats. But it is not the end of insecurity in the southwest or Nigeria as a whole," Barnett said. ___ For more on Africa and development: https://apnews.com/hub/africa-pulse The Associated Press receives financial support for global health and development coverage in Africa from the Gates Foundation. Forecasters advised people to stay hydrated and find places to cool off, warning of temperatures 15 to 25 degrees Fahrenheit (8 to 14 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal in many areas, including at night — especially bad for people's health because their bodies won't have a chance to recover. The heat dome was expected to affect as much as two-thirds of the continental United States. “The heat doesn’t necessarily stop when it’s dark out,” said Josh Adam, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Bismarck, North Dakota, where temperatures will surpass 100 F (37 C) until Tuesday, a dramatic spike for a state where summer temperatures are typically in the 80s. Tynika Smith of Bloomington, Minnesota, handed out frozen towels and wash cloths along with battery-operated fans at encampments of homeless people in nearby St. Paul and will continue next week, when temperatures are forecast to climb into the mid- to high 90s. The residents put the ice packs around their necks and on their heads. “They can’t get into a car with air conditioning or go into a house,” said Smith, who also distributed water, freezer pops, food and hygiene supplies. The encampments are so secluded that it's difficult for the residents to walk or bicycle to cooling centers, she said. There also is little outside shade, while the temperature inside their tents gets even hotter than outdoors. “I can only do so much,” Smith said, “but at least I can help them stay cool for a little bit.” Temperature records expected to be broken The National Weather Service predicted that more than 90 U.S. local temperature records will be tied or broken through Wednesday — with two-thirds of those being overnight heat records. Temperatures were not forecast to drop below 80 F (27 C) at night in Fort Lauderdale, Florida; Miami; Tampa, Florida; Galveston, Texas; and Charleston, South Carolina. The heat dome — formed when high pressure traps hot air while blocking cooling winds and rain — is one of the strongest to affect the Dakotas in 25 years, said Chad Merrill, a senior meteorologist with AccuWeather. Record triple-digit highs were forecast for the weekend in Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho, Montana and the Dakotas. In Helena, Montana, where temperatures were expected to creep above 95 F (35 C), Last Chance Splash Waterpark & Pool was holding a swim meet for hundreds of swimmers. The timing couldn’t be better, as it’s uncommon for Helena to get so hot, said Sean Swingley, assistant manager. “It’s certainly a hot day, but the pool is nice and cool,” Swingley said. “Usually in the summer we have a couple 95 degree days, but it mostly hovers around 85 to 90 in June and July.” Nevada, a state accustomed to hot weather, was even hotter than normal, said Andrew Gorelow, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Las Vegas. The temperature there was expected to hit 111 F (48 C) on Saturday, Gorelow said. Hydrating and finding cool spaces is critical, experts said. They also warned that the heat could spike fire risk in some parts of the country that already are dry, including the Rockies, where Merrill said dry thunderstorms could develop. Climate change is supercharging heat Climate change from the burning of coal, oil and natural gas is causing more intense and longer-lasting heat waves that cover larger areas, scientists say. This year's temperatures also are expected to be affected by El Nino, a natural warming of the equatorial Pacific that alters weather patterns and spikes temperatures across the globe. The current El Nino — which formed last month and is too young to have affected this heat wave much — is expected to rank as among the most intense since the weather service began tracking the phenomena in 1950, experts said. By fall it has an 81% chance of becoming “very strong” — the top category — according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. ___ The Associated Press’ climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. column12: Jakarta (ANTARA) - Kepala Badan Pangan Nasional (Bapanas) sekaligus Menteri Pertanian Andi Amran Sulaiman memastikan fenomena El Nino tidak akan mengganggu ketahanan pangan Indonesia karena pemerintah telah memperkuat cadangan pangan dan mengantisipasi dampaknya sejak dini. "Sekarang alhamdulillah, ini atas arahan Bapak Presiden (Prabowo Subianto) Tidak usah khawatir. El Nino yang dulu lebih dahsyat daripada sekarang. Kemarin katanya bulan empat, tapi (malah ada) banjir. Bulan lima, bulan enam, banjir. Bulan tujuh juga masih ada banjir. Nah, bulan delapan katanya lagi," kata Amran dalam keterangan terkonfirmasi di Jakarta, Selasa. Kesiapsiagaan pemerintah untuk menghadapi fenomena El Nino dipastikan kuat, terutama dari aspek ketersediaan pangan pokok strategis. Prediksi terjadinya El Nino telah ada sejak beberapa bulan lalu, sehingga mitigasi berupa penguatan stok cadangan pangan pemerintah (CPP) menjadi instrumen yang wajib disiapkan. Amran menegaskan kesiapsiagaan tersebut dan mengimbau masyarakat cukup bersikap tenang. Capaian swasembada pangan yang diraih pada era kepemimpinan Presiden Prabowo Subianto merupakan sebuah prestasi bagi kemaslahatan masyarakat. "Ini (prediksinya) ada El Nino Godzilla, bulan empat, ternyata (malah) banjir. Alhamdulillah tidak jadi, tetapi bisa membuat petani takut tanam," kata Amran. Dalam laporan Bapanas, stok CPP dalam bentuk beras yang ada di Perum Bulog berada di angka 5,24 juta ton per 20 Juli. Sementara untuk cadangan pangan pemerintah daerah (CPPD) tingkat provinsi tercatat total 7,35 ribu ton per akhir Juni 2026. Untuk CPPD tingkat kabupaten/kota total ada 13,15 ribu ton yang tersebar di 323 daerah. Di samping itu, stok CPP dalam bentuk jagung pakan per 20 Juli masih terdapat sebanyak 176 ribu ton. Stok jagung pakan ini terus disalurkan kepada peternak unggas melalui program stabilisasi pasokan dan harga pangan (SPHP) dengan harga yang lebih ekonomis. Selanjutnya, stok CPP dalam bentuk minyak goreng 1 ribu kiloliter yang dikelola Perum Bulog dan ID Food. CPP gula konsumsi masih ada sekitar 2,79 ribu ton yang juga ada di Bulog dan ID Food. CPP dalam bentuk daging ayam ada 38 ton di ID Food. Khusus untuk komoditas yang sifatnya perishable atau mudah membusuk atau mudah rusak, seperti cabai, bawang merah, dan telur ayam ras, pemerintah optimis mampu ditopang dari produksi pangan dalam negeri secara reguler. Hal ini karena adanya surplus produksi terhadap kebutuhan konsumsi yang cukup tinggi selama setahun ini. Dia mengatakan berdasarkan laporan Badan Pusat Statistik (BPS), Indeks Perkembangan Harga (IPH) masih cukup baik. Adapun sampai minggu ketiga Juli 2026, hanya empat provinsi yang mengalami kenaikan IPH dan 34 provinsi mengalami penurunan IPH. IPH secara kabupaten/kota pun demikian. Sampai minggu ketiga Juli, BPS melaporkan 69 kabupaten/kota dengan kenaikan IPH, sementara sebanyak 283 kabupaten/kota mengalami penurunan IPH. Keberhasilan tersebut mencakup swasembada jagung dan beras. "Kita bisa wujudkan mimpi kita, gagasan besar Bapak Presiden. Sekarang sudah swasembada beras. Swasembada pangan juga sudah," beber Amran. Menurutnya, manfaat bendungan baru benar-benar dirasakan ketika air mengalir hingga lahan pertanian dan dimanfaatkan masyarakat. "Swasembada pangan, swasembada energi, dan swasembada air memerlukan tata kelola air yang tertib, berkelanjutan, dan benar-benar sampai kepada rakyat. Bendungan adalah hulu dari pelayanan itu,” katanya dalam keterangan tertulis yang dikutip Selasa, 21 Juli 2026. Bendungan Jlantah ini memiliki kapasitas tampung mencapai 11,82 juta meter kubik dengan luas genangan seluas 54,77 hektare. Infrastruktur tersebut juga mampu mereduksi banjir pada area persawahan seluas 87 hektare di Kabupaten Karanganyar. Melalui jaringan irigasi, bendungan tersebut mendukung ketahanan pangan melalui layanan jaringan irigasi yang menjangkau lahan seluas 1.494 hektare. Sebanyak 806 hektare di antaranya telah terlayani melalui jaringan yang tersebar pada 15 daerah irigasi (DI). Ketersediaan air dari bendungan ini juga meningkatkan indeks pertanaman petani dari 172 persen menjadi 272 persen. Kondisi tersebut memungkinkan petani melakukan penanaman lebih sering dalam satu tahun dibandingkan sebelumnya. Selain itu, masih terdapat potensi pengembangan irigasi seluas 688 hektare yang tersebar pada 20 DI. Kemudian, bendungan tersebut juga mendukung program cetak sawah melalui saluran induk Jlantah seluas 229,90 hektare. Bendungan Jlantah ini menyediakan air baku sebesar 150 liter per detik untuk meningkatkan layanan air minum masyarakat. Sehingga, cakupan layanan di tiga kecamatan meningkat dari sebelumnya 20 persen menjadi 100 persen. Infrastruktur tersebut juga mendukung kebutuhan air domestik dengan proyeksi swasembada air mencapai 71,41 persen pada 2040. Selain itu, bendungan memiliki potensi pembangkit listrik sebesar 10,625 megawatt untuk mendukung swasembada energi. Pembangunan Bendungan Jlantah tersebut dilaksanakan Balai Besar Wilayah Sungai (BBWS) Bengawan Solo sejak 2019 hingga 2024. Proyek bernilai Rp1,02 triliun tersebut diharapkan menjadi solusi jangka panjang menghadapi krisis air saat musim kemarau El Nino. AUCKLAND: Australia's Great Barrier Reef is at a very high risk of extreme and widespread bleaching and "ecosystem collapse" linked to this year's El Nino weather phenomenon, top scientists warned on Tuesday (Jul 21). Often dubbed the world's largest living structure, the reef stretches 2,300km along the coast of Queensland state and is a major tourism draw for Australia. This month it avoided being listed as endangered, despite the United Nations reporting "utmost concern" about mass coral bleaching and the impact of climate change. Morgan Pratchett, a marine conservation ecologist at Queensland's James Cook University, told the International Coral Reef Symposium in Auckland, New Zealand, that the "extreme El Nino" posed a significant concern. "It's not outside of the realm of possibility that the next major disturbance will lead to localised species extinctions ... and widespread ecosystem collapse," Pratchett said. This year's El Nino is expected to break records for its overall strength as it warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns. "It's a very high likelihood that we'll see very high severity and large-scale mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef," Pratchett said. UNESCO has been monitoring the reef annually since 2021, when it warned it was at risk of being placed on the list of World Heritage items "in danger". Hard coral cover across the reef declined substantially in 2024-2025, with above-average water temperatures causing the reef's sixth mass coral bleaching event since 2016. Extreme weather, land-based run-off, coastal development and predation by the Crown of Thorns starfish were also placing the reef under pressure. Marine studies professor Ove Hoegh-Guldberg from the University of Queensland said a lack of government action had globally threatened the future of coral reefs around the world. "This could be the precursor to the loss of humans," he said. "If you were on a big boat, like the Titanic, and someone comes up to you and says the boat's going down, you bloody well get on those lifeboats and start acting and do stuff." "We're not doing that. column12: New Delhi: The below-normal rainfall associated with El Nino may be good news for the cotton sector, as officials and industry executives expect farmers in key rain-fed states to shift from water-intensive crops to cotton, helping bridge the current sowing gap. A normal cotton crop would ensure adequate raw material for textile manufacturers and reduce the scope for any increase in textile prices stemming from costlier imported cotton amid ongoing geopolitical tensions. This comes against the backdrop of cotton acreage trailing last year's level. Cotton has been sown over 92.53 lakh hectares as of 17 July, down 5.96% from 98.39 lakh hectares in the corresponding period last year, according to the agriculture ministry's latest weekly sowing data. The development is significant because cotton remains the dominant raw material for India's textile and apparel industry, accounting for around 80% of the fibre consumed by the sector and around 65% of apparel production. - Cotton sowing trails last year by 5.96% amid early-season El Niño uncertainty. - Maharashtra, Gujarat sowing falls; Telangana, Andhra Pradesh post gains this cotton season. - CCI chief expects farmers to shift toward cotton if rainfall stays deficient. - Import duty waiver until October eases supply concerns before new crop arrives. - Ex-Tirupur exporters' head warns global El Niño impact could still disrupt supplies. The initial sowing data also show mixed trends across major cotton-producing states. Maharashtra, the country's largest cotton producer, recorded a 6.82% decline in acreage to 34.21 lakh hectares, while Gujarat saw sowing fall 9.76% to 16.75 lakh hectares. In contrast, Telangana reported a 6.62% increase to 16.64 lakh hectares, and Andhra Pradesh posted a 34.2% jump to 2.75 lakh hectares. The final acreage will be closely watched by the textile industry. Cotton acreage has remained around 115 lakh hectares over the past two years, while production has fallen from 336.6 lakh bales in FY23 to 290.24 lakh bales in FY26, tightening domestic supplies and increasing reliance on imports. Positive for now As of now, the import duty of around 11% on cotton imports has been waived until October 2026. Thereafter, the arrival of the new domestic cotton crop is expected to ease supply concerns. “There is no need to worry for textile manufacturers with respect to the availability of domestic cotton. The acreage is expected to improve, given that El Niño may encourage farmers in cotton-growing states to shift to cotton in the event of deficient rainfall,” said L.K. Gupta, chairman-cum-managing director, Cotton Corporation of India, a public sector undertaking under the Ministry of Textiles. “There is a reason for this. Other crops may not yield well under deficient rainfall, but in the case of cotton, there is always a good chance of getting a reasonable yield even if rainfall is deficient.” Gupta further said that CCI is working closely with textile mills and making concerted efforts to supply cotton directly to manufacturers rather than traders, to help keep textile prices under control while ensuring farmers receive better prices for their produce. Industry executives also echoed the assessment, saying current sowing trends do not indicate any major risk to cotton output. “The sowing season is still at an early stage, and planting is picking up. The acreage gap is expected to narrow over the coming weeks. So there is no need to worry about cotton production,” an executive at a leading textile company said on condition of anonymity due to operational sensitivities. El Nino may hit imports Former Tirupur Exporters' Association president Raja M. Shanmugam, however, said that El Niño remains a global phenomenon and could still disrupt cotton supplies if production declines in major producing countries. “The El Niño effect is not limited to India; it is going to be global. If there is a shortfall in production, there are chances of supply disruptions, resulting in higher raw material prices. In that case, the government will need to come out with corrective measures to support the industry,” Shanmugam said. “In such a scenario, the role of CCI is going to be crucial. Since not all spinning mills can buy and store cotton for long periods, CCI should create a buffer stock and release cotton to mills from time to time at the MSP (Minimum Support Price). The cotton should be sold only to genuine users, not traders, as traders often engage in speculation and many are backed by foreign investors,” he added. Farmers in key cotton-growing states also said deficient but well-distributed rainfall could encourage a shift towards cotton. Ishvar Bhai Chavda, a cotton farmer from Gujarat's Morbi district, said farmers would prefer cotton if rainfall proves deficient. Chavda, who cultivates cotton on his 10-acre farm, has already completed sowing on his entire land, while many of his fellow farmers are also preparing to sow the crop, often referred to as 'white gold'. Another farmer, Ganesh Nanote from Maharashtra's Vidarbha region, said lower but timely rainfall is beneficial for the cotton crop. "If rainfall is lower but arrives on time, cotton production will increase, along with the sowing area. Soybean, which farmers often cultivate as a diversification crop alongside cotton, requires more water. So, farmers who would otherwise grow soybean are likely to shift to cotton," Nanote said. Imports of raw cotton rose 54.9% year-on-year to $1.89 billion in FY26, according to DGFT data. In contrast, exports declined 33.9% to $436.37 million during the same period. ||| SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Weeklong rainstorms blamed on El Nino that have battered Chile have killed at least 10 people as authorities raced on Tuesday to reach more than 100,000 cut off by flash floods in what has been one of the country's worst weather disasters in decades. Torrential rains and strong winds continued to lash the usually arid northern regions of Atacama and Coquimbo, where the government of President José Antonio Kast declared a state of emergency on Monday. Authorities said the storms have also injured 16 people and displaced over 4,000 others, with 1,031 staying in emergency shelters. Thousands more have been left without electricity or drinking water. The rainfall has so far destroyed 81 homes and damaged more than 20,000. Chile's national disaster response service, Senapred, has sent out hundreds of evacuation alerts to 10 out of the country's 16 regions. Swollen rivers and flooded roads have stranded 104,271 people, Senapred reported, warning that overwhelmed rivers will remain a threat even when the rainfall eases. "River levels do not necessarily rise at the same time precipitation is falling," said Alicia Cebrián, the head of Senapred. "Water accumulates in the foothill areas, which means river levels can continue rising even hours after the storm system has passed." Meteorologists attribute the deluge in Chile to the return of El Nino, a powerful, naturally occurring phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that drives temperatures higher and exacerbates extreme weather events. El Niño is typically associated with heavier rainfall in parts of southern South America. ||| Indian consumer goods companies are expected to report pressure on first-quarter profit margins, as the Iran war-fuelled higher raw material costs outweighed benefits from resilient demand and price hikes, brokerages said. Commodities expected to see price spikes include cocoa — and hence chocolate, coffee, rice and sugar. On the domestic front, the main concerns are focused on summer grain crops, notably the staple maize. The effects will be uneven, with some supply chains cushioned by ample stocks. And a few agricultural regions may get a boost from the good rains that the weather pattern typically brings to them. But there are two dark clouds of uncertainty swirling over soft commodity markets that could herald seismic price shocks. The first is the ongoing Iran war, which is creating a perfect agricultural price storm in tandem with El Niño. “The Strait of Hormuz conflict has simultaneously disrupted fertiliser supply chains, compounding weather-driven yield risk with input cost stress, which is a combination not seen in prior El Niño cycles,” said Aneeka Gupta, director of macroeconomic research at asset manager WisdomTree Europe, in a recent note. “The last time a major El Niño hit (2023-2024), markets were watching. Cocoa rallied 250%. Sugar hit its highest price in over a decade. Rice exporters shut their borders. Those events felt dramatic at the time, but they unfolded before the US-Iran war, before the fertiliser crunch, before the warming baseline had climbed another notch.” The other cloud is the unprecedented nature of this El Niño, which is likely to take commodity markets into uncharted waters. “With the July runs now in from 667 ensemble members across 14 different seasonal forecast models, it looks like this year’s El Niño is not only very likely to be the strongest event since reliable records began — it may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin,” climate scientist Zeke Hausfather wrote last week in his influential newsletter Climate Brink. The trigger for El Niño is a warming of surface sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific. Hausfather, a co-author of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), noted that the “temperature anomalies” — climate-speak for the deviation in sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific from their long-term average — currently stand at 3.6°C above the norm, “roughly 0.8°C hotter than the prior record of 2.75°C set in 2015-16”. “For context, the gap between the strongest and the fifth-strongest El Niño of the past 150 years is only about 0.5°C. The models are forecasting something outside the envelope of anything we have ever observed.” If that is the case, then commodity markets and consumers worldwide need to brace for an event that is “outside the envelope”. Record prices The last El Niño saw orange juice futures and cocoa prices scale new peaks while coffee reached a record high in 2025. “Every strong El Niño in the past 55 years has reduced global cocoa production,” WisdomTree’s Gupta noted. West Africa, which accounts for about two-thirds of global cocoa supplies, is already feeling the effects of El Niño, according to Oxford Economics Africa senior economist Leeuwner Esterhuysen. Heavy rainfall and floods have hit the region, and there are fears that a combination of drought and deluge will follow. “Field observations in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana point to weak pod development, with initial estimates suggesting Côte d’Ivoire’s next harvest could fall by roughly 20% during the 2026/27 harvest season,” said Esterhuysen in a recent note. But it’s not all doom and gloom for chocolate lovers. Swiss-based Barry Callebaut, the world’s largest chocolate maker, said earlier this month that the potential supply shock from El Niño would be minimised by ample stocks and surpluses — a stark contrast from the previous one, which coincided with deficits. This mirrors the situation regarding South African maize. In the wake of the last La Niña — which typically brings good rains to this region, while El Niño heralds drought — South Africa’s maize harvest this year is estimated to be a record 17.3 million tonnes, well over annual domestic consumption of around 12 million tonnes. Both scenarios point to surplus supplies that should help to contain the price shocks, which in the case of maize in South Africa hit poor and working-class households the hardest. South Africa’s dam and moisture levels are also at decent levels for the most part. But this relatively benign outlook could be in for a rude awakening given the forecast severity of this El Niño, which is gaining strength at a menacing pace. “The 2026 event is developing faster than 1997-98, the previous gold standard for explosive El Niño onsets,” Hausfather ominously noted. It will also stick around for a while. The US Weather Service, in its latest forecast, says there is a 97% chance that it will not fade before the northern spring/austral autumn — so the entire summer grain growing season in South Africa will take place under its scorching presence. And if it reappears quickly again, the outlook will be grim. Good maize stocks and favourable dam and moisture levels will evaporate at some point, leaving the South African economy high and dry. ‘A great blow’ “An El Niño drought that extends beyond one season will deal a great blow to the economy, with food inflation likely rising into double digits before easing,” said Reezwana Sumad, senior research analyst at Nedbank. “This is not our base case, but it is certainly something we will watch very closely in the coming months.” South African cattle producers, already reeling from the foot-and-mouth disease outbreaks, will also feel the heat as feed costs rise and grazing lands wither — but at least the fields are in good nick ahead of time, and the surplus of yellow maize used for animal feed will help. “With irrigation dams at reasonable levels, and maize prices predicted to stay reasonably stable as a result of the ample carryover stock, the cost of feed is not expected to increase exponentially,” said Zhann Meyer, the sector lead for agriculture at Nedbank. But an extension beyond one season would trigger a mass slaughter of herds. This would initially depress South African meat prices, but they would spike afterwards as the supply glut would be replaced by scarcity. This fast-developing El Niño is already wreaking havoc. Beyond west Africa, devastating floods linked to the weather phenomenon have seen Chile declare a state of catastrophe. And south and southeast Asia are bracing for hotter and drier conditions that will adversely affect rice, sugar, coffee and palm oil production. South Africa is also bracing for hotter and drier conditions, and such trends elsewhere will also affect the price of stuff we eat and drink. Soft commodity markets are heating up towards the boiling point, and the global economy and consumers worldwide are going to get burnt. DM

column12: The forum was established through the collective efforts of local civil society organizations (CSOs) and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to foster stronger collaboration among government institutions, the private sector, smallholder farmers, academia, civil society organizations, and development partners in accelerating improvements to sustainable palm oil governance in Central Sulawesi. Member of Commission III of the Central Sulawesi Provincial Regional House of Representatives (DPRD), H Musliman, emphasized that the forum should serve not only as a platform for exchanging ideas but also as a catalyst for tangible progress in the province. “We hope this forum will generate meaningful breakthroughs for the palm oil sector in Central Sulawesi. Collaboration among all stakeholders is the key, and together we can advance the sustainable development of the province’s palm oil industry,” he said. Palm oil is one of Indonesia’s largest foreign exchange-earning commodities, generating between US$20 billion and US$27.75 billion annually and accounting for approximately 12% of the country’s non-oil and gas exports. The industry contributes around 1.6% of Indonesia’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP), generates tens of trillions of rupiah in tax revenues, and provides direct employment to more than 4.5 million people. Echoing this view, Jen Kurnia Gembu, Head of the Legal Division at the Central Sulawesi Provincial Secretariat, expressed the Provincial Government’s support for the establishment of the forum. He described it as a strategic initiative to strengthen assistance in addressing challenges facing the palm oil sector while ensuring its long-term sustainability. According to him, the industry continues to face numerous challenges requiring support in regulatory compliance, governance, and the resolution of field-level issues. Strengthened collaboration among stakeholders through the forum will therefore be essential in developing sustainable solutions. “In principle, the Legal Bureau of the Central Sulawesi Provincial Secretariat fully supports the establishment of the Sustainable Palm Oil Multi-Stakeholder Forum. Many challenges remain in the palm oil sector that require coordinated assistance to ensure sustainable management,” Gembu said. He further noted that government leadership will play a critical role in coordinating stakeholders, ensuring legal certainty, and developing policies that support sustainable palm oil governance throughout the province. “The government’s role is essential in coordinating all stakeholders so that challenges can be addressed collaboratively while advancing sustainable palm oil development in Central Sulawesi,” he added. Professor Mohamad Ahlis Djirimu, an academic from Tadulako University (Untad) in Palu, emphasized that collaboration among all stakeholders is fundamental to achieving a sustainable palm oil industry. “What we need is stronger synergy among corporations, the provincial government, and district and municipal governments. Without collaboration, we will not be able to maximize the benefits of the palm oil industry,” he said. He also noted that downstream development of the palm oil industry in Central Sulawesi continues to face challenges because most processing facilities are located outside the province. As a result, transporting fresh fruit bunches (FFB) from several production areas becomes less efficient due to long transportation distances. As the world approaches the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) review, he stressed that palm oil development in Central Sulawesi must continue to uphold sustainability principles by protecting both workers and the environment. “Workers’ rights must be protected, including the right to organize. We must also promote inclusiveness, particularly by safeguarding the rights of women workers. Global expectations will increasingly focus on sustainability issues in the years ahead,” he added. Azmi Sirajudin, Executive Director of Ekonesia, stated that the establishment of the forum marks an important milestone in creating a collaborative platform capable of aligning diverse interests in the development of a sustainable palm oil sector in Central Sulawesi. “We expect this forum to become a common platform for strengthening communication, enhancing coordination, and fostering collaboration among all stakeholders so that palm oil governance in Central Sulawesi becomes more effective, sustainable, and beneficial for local communities,” Azmi said. He explained that the forum is also aligned with the Central Sulawesi Provincial Government’s vision of achieving prosperous, equitable, advanced, and sustainable development through its Nine BERANI development agenda, particularly the BERANI Makmur (Prosperity) mission. “The forum will perform several strategic functions, including serving as a facilitator to strengthen the capacity of independent smallholders in implementing sustainable agricultural practices, as well as acting as a mediator to facilitate dialogue and resolve disputes among stakeholders,” he explained. In addition, the forum will serve as a catalyst to encourage active stakeholder participation in sustainable palm oil management and as an accelerator to support the achievement of national strategic priorities, including the Smallholder Palm Oil Replanting Program (PSR), implementation of the Indonesian Sustainable Palm Oil (ISPO) standard, downstream industry development, and the transition toward deforestation-free, environmentally responsible, and human rights-respecting palm oil production. “Through this forum, we aim to ensure that every stakeholder has a platform for dialogue, joint problem-solving, and supporting the implementation of sustainable palm oil practices in Central Sulawesi. Collaboration is the key to building an inclusive and globally competitive palm oil sector,” Azmi concluded. The Central Sulawesi Sustainable Palm Oil Multi-Stakeholder Forum is expected to become a collaborative platform that strengthens stakeholder partnerships while supporting the achievement of sustainable palm oil development targets across the province. The call to prioritise practical relief comes as almost half the state is predicted to be in drought by September, and farmers plan production outcomes with forecasts of El Nino weather patterns in mind. NSW Farmers Grains Committee Chair Justin Everitt said members are not satisfied with the current framework - with many reporting more tangible assistance on the ground was necessary. "Drought responses need to be practical with meaningful relief measures that support farmers manage and recover from drought, and prepare for the next one which is always just around the corner," Mr Everitt said. "Incentives for on-farm infrastructure improvements such as silos, livestock water infrastructure and containment areas, is one solution proposed." "Other ones include fixed cost fee relief for businesses such as the waiving of road usage charges for trucks and a federal and state government subsidy for shire rates." NSW Farmers will advocate that the NSW Government provide dollar-for-dollar matched drought assistance grants for drought-affected farming businesses for water infrastructure improvements, fodder purchases up to $15,000 and financial planning services. "Fodder grants would be a far better drought support measure than a freight subsidy." Farmers are also keen for a return to formal drought declarations when there is sustained low rainfall (5 - 10 percent of historical records) over a sustained time period (6 - 12 months). "NSW Farmers will continue to advocate for practical drought measures that make sure that State and Federal government policy settings are fit-for-purpose, to ensure that farm businesses where can effectively respond and recover from drought - especially where those severe conditions are beyond what can be prepared for." ||| It is the silly season of elections again. The Johor state election has come and gone. Next up is Negeri Sembilan, followed by Malacca. Then, perhaps early next year, the general election for the whole country. So much hustle and bustle. The usual break-up of makeshift coalitions is under way. Perikatan Nasional is under threat: Bersatu and Pas are no longer best friends forever. Part of Bersatu has already broken away. No split from PKR looks imminent, but a few top leaders have resigned and formed a new party, Bersama. It contested the Johor election and was trounced – all its candidates lost their deposits. Before that, several former DAP leaders had said they might quit to join Bersama too. And the leader nicknamed ‘Mr Keluar Sekejap’ (Mr Step-Out-Briefly) – who once quit Umno – has said he is still keen on becoming prime minister one day. So he has rejoined Umno. No surprise there. My little crystal ball predicts that neither the state elections nor the coming general election will solve the problem of a hung parliament, where no single party or coalition wins a majority. Instead, expect more horse-trading and repeated attempts to cobble together a grander coalition – a ‘Unity 2.0’ government of sorts – just to survive any vote of no confidence. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member This means survival and expediency will prevail over any reform agenda again, whatever the parties and their leaders promise on the campaign trail. Be warned: they will not be able to deliver, because building a majority may mean including people who have spent their political careers opposing the very reforms on offer. Worse, the grand coalition might have grand names like ‘Unity’ and ‘Madani’, but that does not not disguise the fact that it includes leaders who have faced corruption allegations or charges – as with the appointment of the Umno chief as deputy PM, whose charges were later dropped. A future Unity 2.0 government could include leaders like the Johor Umno chief, who declared he would not work with the DAP to form the Johor state government – even though both parties are supposed allies in the federal ‘unity government’. With coalition partners like that, who needs enemies? It could also include people who want to amend the law to allow for the appointment – rather than election – of political leaders in this 21st Century, nearly 70 years into Malaysia’s electoral democracy. And, of course, the coalition will include politicians who will readily stir up ethnic and religious sentiment to score points, deepening disunity. Some will want to join the Unity 2.0 government simply to campaign for the release of their convicted former leader. (Reflect on this for a moment: former Prime Minister Najib Razak was found guilty in 2020 of criminal breach of trust and abuse of power for illegally receiving RM42m misappropriated from a unit of 1MDB. He was convicted by nine judges across three levels of the judiciary, all of whom ruled against him unanimously. He was then sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined RM210m. His supporters are pushing for his release – and we may end up working with them in a Unity 2.0 government?) No wonder reforms have been few and far between under this ‘Madani’ unity government. Reforms delayed for over 60 years Umno-Barisan Nasional’s electoral dominance shaped every part of Malaysia’s political system, leaving its mark for over 60 years. Beyond the two-thirds parliamentary majority that let it amend the 1957 constitution at will, Umno-BN influenced the workings of the entire bureaucracy: the civil service, the army, the police and a judicial system that collapsed the roles of the Attorney General’s Chambers and the public prosecutor. Umno-BN also influenced public policy, the allocation of public funds, and who won government tenders to implement this or that policy – invariably a crony or two. It also shaped how government worked, not just federally but at state and local level. It is right to demand leadership changes in the country’s top institutions – the bureaucracy, the judiciary, government-linked companies – just as we demand changes in the government of the day. But changing personnel is not enough. Sixty years of Umno-BN rule call for a revamp of the whole system, or what people now call the entire Umno-BN ecosystem. Let’s step back to understand how we ended up in this situation. Essentially, it is because we are still stuck in Old Politics, even though we now have a New Economy and a New Society. New Economy, New Society As a scholar-activist studying Malaysian politics, I’ve been waiting a long time for New Politics to arrive. The economy, meanwhile, has been transformed beyond recognition. Growth and government revenue once rested on commodities – first rubber and tin, then tropical timber and palm oil, then offshore oil and gas. Today, the economy runs on services and manufacturing, especially electrical and electronics. These sectors contribute most of Malaysia’s revenue and attract the bulk of foreign direct investment. That economic shift has reshaped Malaysian society too. Fewer people work in agriculture now. More work in manufacturing and services. The ranks of managers, administrators and registered professionals and technicians have grown. The civil service has expanded to 1.8 million – arguably too large for a population of over 30 million. In 2016, primary school enrolment stood at 97%, upper secondary at 94%, and post-secondary at 17%. An estimated half a million teachers and administrators worked across 10,000 schools, educating five million students nationwide – a huge leap from what the peninsula inherited from the British at its independence in 1957. In 1958, we had only a branch campus of the University of Malaya in Pantai Valley (the main campus was in Singapore). By 1980, there were five public universities; by 2015, 27, plus 32 polytechnics and 84 public community colleges. Today, there are also 47 private universities and university colleges, with over half a million students enrolled in tertiary education. Not surprisingly, the educated, urban middle class now makes up about a third of Malaysia’s population. Thanks to the New Economic Policy (NEP), this middle class is strikingly multi-ethnic – unlike before, when the educated middle class was largely non-Malay. One key effect of this new class is that ethnic and other social groups have grown more fragmented too. Instead of one popularly acclaimed leader per ethnic group, there are now many. Meanwhile, social media has given rise to countless spokespeople for any given cause or group. So, since independence, and after over 50 years of the NEP, Malaysia has built a New Economy and a New Society. But where is the New Politics? Whither New Politics? Malaysia’s Old politics, most agree, was dominated by a small group of elites presiding over ethnic-based parties, linked at the top through a multi-ethnic coalition. All of the BN parties got into business too – banks, media empires, construction conglomerates, education ventures. As long as these parties doubled as systems of patronage that fed members down the pyramid, the elites’ control over the rest was secure. So, a defining feature of Malaysia’s Old Politics was also patronage and the prevalence of ‘money politics’. New Politics, one hoped, would be multi-ethnic and inclusive. It would shed money politics and patronage, allow free and fair elections, and open the door to democratic participation. Above all, one hoped Umno-BN – in power for 60 years – would finally be displaced by an alternative multi-ethnic coalition. So there was real excitement when the 2018 general election ushered in the Pakatan Harapan coalition led by Dr Mahathir Mohamad. Many hoped for deeper democracy: free and fair elections restored, elected local government brought back, and reform of key institutions – the judiciary, the police, the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission, the universities, the entire education system. Coercive laws, one prayed, would be repealed too. Perhaps there would be more consultation with the people – through parliamentary select committees – before policy was made. Maybe new royal commissions of inquiry would investigate chronic problems, starting with widespread corruption and money politics. A commission to examine the civil service seemed overdue too, given how much autonomy and professionalism it had lost after 60 years of Umno-BN rule. At the very least, one hoped the civil service would adopt evidence-based policymaking. Instead, the opposite happened! The result of the 2018 election was undone by the ‘Sheraton Move’ backdoor coup. Political intrigue and instability followed. Rather than decisions being made transparently, in Parliament or at the ballot box, politicians struck deals among themselves. Breakaway parties formed overnight. New coalitions with names like ‘Gabungan This’ and ‘Something-Plus’ sprang up. In a single decade, Malaysia changed its prime minister six times. Thank heavens for the alternative media, where we can voice our dissatisfaction. Because so many institutions have been compromised, there is little other room left to manoeuvre to safeguard our democracy. Unfortunately, ordinary people, like their leaders, have had to increasingly turn to the Agong to resolve political intrigue and instability. This is not the New Politics we envisioned when the New Economy and New Society arrived. This version of New Politics has been corrupted. Corruption and Umno-BN’s collapse The main cause of Malaysia’s current political predicament is the implosion of Umno. Before that came the near-disappearance of the MCA, MIC, PPP, Gerakan and the rest of BN’s 14 parties, including those from Sabah and Sarawak. Umno-BN – or its predecessor, the Alliance – had won every general election since 1957. Now it has collapsed. That is not to say Umno-BN was ever as central to the system as it seemed; its importance was overstated. It mattered for political stability mainly because so many other institutions had already been undermined or compromised. The judiciary, the Attorney General’s Chambers, the public prosecutor and their aides, the civil service from the chief secretary down, the police and other law enforcement units, all answerable to the executive, Parliament and so on had all been compromised. They were no longer fully competent, accountable or transparent. The trigger for Umno-BN’s collapse was unprecedented corruption within the party. A rot had set in at the very top. Former Umno president and former Prime Minister Najib Razak was found guilty in 2020 of criminal breach of trust and abuse of power. Shamelessly, he appealed and re-appealed his conviction. Malaysia had become a kleptocracy par excellence. To restore democratic momentum, root out corruption at every level, rebuild political stability and maintain economic development, we cannot simply keep holding elections and hoping fresh faces and new party names will change things. Nor is the answer to restore the old system of stability held together by a single dominant party like Umno-BN, which ruled for six decades. Despite Umno’s recent success in the Johor state election, do not for a moment assume it is on its way back to the top. We must not let that happen! We need real reform instead – restructuring the political system by decentralising power, revenue and participation downwards. Global trend towards decentralisation There is a worldwide trend towards greater decentralisation, in developed and developing countries alike. Older federations in the West – the US, Canada, Switzerland – did not provide for a third, elected tier of government – local government – in their original constitutions. But they have since passed laws allowing relatively autonomous local authorities, such as New York City, Greater London and Greater Manchester. In Spain, greater autonomy has gone to the regions through the creation of Autonomous Communities. Unlike these older federations, developing countries have usually included provisions for elected local government into their independence constitutions. South Africa’s 1996 constitution, for example, split power and resources three ways, equally, between the centre, the provinces and local government. India amended its constitution in 1994 to reserve seats in local, or panchayat, elections for women and for ‘scheduled tribes’. Ethiopia has four tiers of government: alongside the centre, the state and local government, there is a district-level woreda. Southeast Asia Across Southeast Asia, although Malaysia is the only federal country in the region, a process of decentralising power and revenue to local government has taken place. In the Philippines, after Ferdinand Marcos’s martial law ended in the 1986 People Power Revolution, Filipinos adopted a new constitution in 1987, followed by a Local Government Code in 1991. Functions in agriculture, health, environment, social welfare and public works were transferred to local governments, whose executives and legislatures were also elected. Civil society groups, including women’s organisations, gained seats on local government committees overseeing development planning, schools, policing and contracts. Local government units were also given 40% of internal revenue, up from 20%, along with the right to tax residents – on condition they kept services running and paid the civil servants under their charge. In Indonesia, no new constitution followed the 1997-98 Reformasi movement, but there were many amendments. These allowed the shift from military to civilian rule, free and fair elections, and the restoration of civil liberties to assemble, associate and speak freely. The police were separated from the army, and anti-corruption laws were passed. Two new local government laws followed in 1999. The first transferred power and functions from the centre to local governments, including metropolitan areas, bypassing some 300 provincial governments. An estimated 10,000 functions and responsibilities were devolved – in public health, education, welfare, land, natural resources, transport, public works and utilities. By 2001, 2.25 million civil servants had been transferred to local government too. The second rebalanced fiscal arrangements between the centre and the regions. Revenue from natural resources – oil, gas, timber, mining – was shared with local governments, with no ‘one size fits all’ formula. Local authorities ended up with more revenue than before, and were often allowed to introduce their own taxes and fees to raise revenue. In return, they took on responsibility for the salaries of civil servants in local government, infrastructure and other local functions. Mega-projects once decided in Jakarta without consulting local governments have been stopped. Local authorities can now reject centrally proposed mega-projects, and some have cancelled old licences the centre had previously issued. Apparently, this ‘big bag of reforms’ led to a chaotic situation. The reforms were too widespread and too fast. Confusion grew over the roles of provinces, districts (kabupaten) and local government. So amendments to regional governance laws followed in 2004, returning some powers to the districts. Another law that year required mayors, district chiefs and village heads all to be elected. In 2014, a further law on village governance required 30% of village officials to be women, to boost women’s participation in decision-making. In effect, the new laws pushed reform down to local governments, with additional revenue and staff to perform the functions devolved to them. Local elections became mandatory. Interestingly, they opened the door to newcomers such as Joko Widodo (Jokowi), who won the mayoralty of Solo, then the governorship of Jakarta, on his way to becoming Indonesia’s president. Malaysia Malaysia is the only Southeast Asian country that calls itself federal. But its federalism is highly centralised. In most federations, social functions such as housing, local transport, public health, primary and secondary education, social welfare, labour, the arts, culture and religion sit with the states or local government. In Malaysia, the centre controls most of these, with only a few shared with the states. Federal systems typically rely on federal-state commissions where the centre and its constituent units meet to iron out problems – what might be called the five Cs: consult, coordinate, cooperate, resolve conflict and adapt to change. Malaysia has only three major commissions: finance, land and local government. India, by contrast, has over 10. Malaysia also gave Sabah and Sarawak greater autonomy at the outset, under the Malaysia Agreement 1963 (MA63). But that autonomy has eroded over time. Rebalancing federal-state relations has been a major demand of both states in return for staying in the Madani ‘unity government’. But several of their demands remain unmet. Penang’s Municipal Council of George Town was the first local authority to hold elections in 1951. Local elections for municipalities, and big and small towns in other states followed. Local council elections were also held in most of the new villages created in the early 1950s. All were suspended in 1965, during ‘Confrontation’ with Indonesia. A royal commission chaired by Senator Athi Nahappan then reviewed the workings of the local governments and found that local councils were performing well. It recommended that local elections resume. But the Local Government Act 1976 abolished all local elections. The government, in effect, rejected its own royal commission’s advice. Since then, the local governments’ role has also shrunk. The George Town City Council once ran an island-wide bus service. Adults used it to get to work, and children, including me, rode it to school. Its health department ran a network of public clinics. Nurses visited new mothers at home. Health department inspectors checked markets and public spaces to control pests. The council also cleaned roads and drains and, collected rubbish and solid waste. It treated sewage before releasing the treated water back into rivers and drains. From the 1970s, following the New Economic Policy and a push towards privatisation, many of these services were taken from local government and tendered to bumiputra individuals and companies or to federal bodies. Water supply, for instance, is now regulated federally. It is time to reverse that centralisation and privatisation of those public utilities. Local governments can run these services more efficiently than Putrajaya or the private sector. Rebuilding democracy from below Why is local government matter so important? Simply put, it can capture the interest and energy of ordinary people, including women. Local government is about clean markets and green, open spaces in neighbourhoods. It is about fighting local crime and having a say in how schools and health services are run. Firefighting, clean roads and drains, and the fight against corruption can also be handled at the local level. Local government can even foster improved relations between ethnic groups at the local level. Above all, decentralised local government provides the local community more avenues to participate in decisions that shape everyday life and livelihoods. Fewer people now care about the jostling for power in Washington, Westminster, the Japanese Diet or Putrajaya. Local election turnouts are rising in many places even as those for national elections fall. (Alas, Malaysia has had no local elections to measure after they were abolished in 1976.) Consider the excitement around the recent mayoral race in New York, won by Zohran Mamdani, or the equivalent contest in Boston, won by Michelle Wu, a lawyer, pianist and daughter of immigrant parents. In Britain, Greater Manchester’s Andy Burnham has just become the country’s new Prime Minister. And in Indonesia, Jokowi – a furniture-shop owner with no political background – created much excitement during his campaign to win the mayoralty of Solo, then the Jakarta governorship, before emerging as Indonesia’s most compelling political figure since Reformasi. If we want to offer people hope, build participatory democracy, and get clean, accountable, transparent government, we need to consolidate local government and rebuild from the bottom up. At a time when public trust in those who once promised reforms has worn thin – not least because of the compromises forced by hung parliaments – we should push for decentralisation to the local government level. We should use this period of ‘instability’ to decentralise. Perhaps work with Sabah and Sarawak. It is worth distinguishing decentralisation to the local level from the question of restoring local elections. If both happen together, that is a bonus. But given how reluctant most parties in the unity government are about reviving local elections, the two do not need to be tied together. Decentralise first; push for local elections later. With decentralisation, we can push towards further democratisation and other reforms. Without it, we are stuck: no democratisation, no reform, no political stability. The region, equivalent in size to the farmland of Western Europe, has been hit hard since 2020 by drought, which slashed yields and ravaged farmer finances. The 120 million acres of prairie farmland produce the world’s biggest canola crop, are often the largest source of spring wheat, and the main global supplier of myriad smaller crops, including lentils and mustard. Ohrtman’s firm analyzes an array of agronomic indicators to assess the agricultural situation, from soil moisture conditions to the state of the vegetative canopy on the fields to the weather in micro-regions, much of it using satellite data. This year, most farmers have received beneficial rainfall, reversing periods of extreme dryness that hit large areas in recent years, providing not just enough moisture for the present needs of the crops but also building reserves that could carry many all the way to harvest. A few more showers could allow most farmers to produce an excellent crop. column12: As Hurricane Fausto continues its track toward the Hawaiian islands, residents are being urged to use the weekend to prepare for potential flooding, evacuations and power outages. Fausto is expected to become the first tropical cyclone of the 2026 hurricane season to impact the islands this year, according to National Weather Service meteorologist Matthew Foster, although it is forecast to diminish to a lesser tropical storm when it reaches Hawaii early next week. The hurricane season began in June and lasts through Nov. 30, Foster said, adding the most storm activity in the Central Pacific Basin is typically during the months of August and September. FORECAST UPDATE: Fausto to bring high surf, possible heavy rain and strong winds to Hawaii The Central Pacific Hurricane Center predicts the region will see five to 13 named cyclones, with a strong El Nino cycle making a higher number of storms more likely. As of Friday evening, Fausto was a Category 2 hurricane — the second of five severity levels on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. The weather system’s strength should downgrade to that of a tropical storm by the time it makes direct contact with the islands Monday night or Tuesday, Foster said. But Fausto’s exact path and intensity as it approaches the islands remains uncertain. Fausto’s center is expected to track just north of the islands, but a track farther south could bring greater risk of stronger winds and heavier rainfall to Hawaii, Friday’s forecast said. On Oahu, residents should expect showers possibly beginning Monday evening through Wednesday. Tropical storm wind speeds range from between 39 and 73 mph, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “In terms of impacts to Hawaii, tropical storm conditions will kind of be the worst-case scenario. We’re not anticipating it to be a hurricane the time it gets here,” Foster said. “The strongest wind should stay north of the state, but there’s still a lot that can that can happen and it’s way too close to really make that call.” As of Friday evening, there were no watches or warnings in effect for Oahu related to the storm. Foster said residents should be prepared for “the big three” — rain, wind and surf. Flooding impacts from potential heavy rainfall and possible thunderstorms are the biggest concern, he said, while wind may not be as much of an issue with this system. The latest forecast predicts swells will reach Hawaii well in advance of the cyclone, which is expected to produce high surf and dangerous rip currents. Surf is expected to build across east-facing shores of the eastern end of the state Sunday, spreading west Sunday night into Monday and continuing to build Tuesday as Fausto approaches the islands. According to Foster, swells could potentially reach “advisory level” of around 10 feet on east- facing shores. “The good news is this (storm) is moving through pretty quickly, so it won’t be one that’s multiple days of rain,” he added. “It should just kind of come through, and it’ll be maybe a day or day-and-a-half where it’s impacting us before it moves off to the west.” The Weather Service is closely monitoring Fausto with state and local officials, Foster said, and all are encouraging residents to get prepared and go over emergency plans. Honolulu Mayor Rick Blangiardi advised residents to ensure disaster supply kits are stocked and to sign up for emergency alerts via hnlalert.gov or by texting “HNLALERT” to 888777. “Preparedness is the best defense against any emergency,” Blangiardi said in a Friday news release. Supply kits should include food, water, medications and essential items to last at least 14 days for each family member and pet. Emergency plans should include securing important documents and having an evacuation plan for those who live in coastal or flood-prone areas. More information on disaster preparedness can be found at honolulu.gov/dem. Hawaii Emergency Management Agency communications director Kiele Amundson said the agency is closely monitoring the storm with local, state and federal partners and reiterated the importance of preparedness. Hawaiian Electric Co. is also focused on Fausto and preparing for potential impacts, the utility said in a Friday news release. HECO said residents should buy extra batteries and ensure emergency equipment, such as flashlights, emergency generators, battery-powered radios, lightsticks and lanterns are working properly. People dependent on electric medical equipment should check backup facilities, make a plan for where to go if evacuations occur and bring medications and medical equipment to the hospital or other emergency shelter should that be necessary. Portable generators should be placed in a well-ventilated area outside the home, HECO said. If using a ladder during a storm, residents should make sure it’s placed at least 10 feet away from power lines. TVs should be turned off and unplugged before lowering or removing TV antennae or satellite dishes. Emergency officials with Hawaii and Maui counties also urged residents to prepare over the weekend, including trimming vegetation surrounding homes, securing or removing outdoor items and clearing debris from drainage areas. “Readiness is a kakou effort,” Maui County Mayor Richard Bissen said in a news release. “We encourage everyone to prepare their families, pets, neighbors and friends, and to check in on vulnerable community members, including kupuna, individuals with disabilities and our unsheltered ohana.”

The new tariffs announced in recent days take effect just as temporary 10% worldwide tariffs expired, and critics say they are less about cracking down on forced labor than they are a way to replace those tariffs. The expired tariffs were themselves a temporary replacement for worldwide tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February. The tariffs were levied on countries that the U.S. says either don’t have or don’t effectively enforce a forced-labor import ban. The affected countries, which account for 99% of U.S. imports, were quick to protest, calling the Trump administration’s claims unfounded and arbitrary, as nations with vastly different records on forced labor received the same tariff level. The U.S. spent four months investigating but gave few details on how it arrived at the tariff rates, which are either 10% or 12.5%. Sidestepping Congress The tariffs were levied under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 on countries that the U.S. determined had failed “to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.” During President Donald Trump ‘s first term, he cited Section 301 to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese imports amid a dispute over the sharp-elbowed tactics Beijing was using to challenge America’s technological dominance. The U.S. is also using 301 powers to counter what it calls unfair Chinese practices in the shipbuilding industry. “The 301s allow a permanent tariff without going to Congress to settle the dispute,” said Barry Appleton, a law professor and co-director of New York Law School’s Center for International Law. “That’s what all of this is about. The president doesn’t want to knock on the front door of Congress, so he’s trying every side door and every unlatched window to get in.” Little evidence that countries failed to enforce import bans The office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) said it consulted with all 60 economies under investigation and held two rounds of public hearings, elicited more than 2,100 public comments, and had “engagement” with its trading partners about what they were doing to combat forced labor bans. It didn’t detail its talks with the countries, saying those were confidential. Experts say it is fairly straightforward to investigate whether a country has a ban or not, but it is difficult to determine the government’s exact rationale for each country’s failure to enforce import bans. “There’s not a lot of hard evidence there,” said Scott Lincicome, vice president for general economics and trade policy at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank. “It’s pretty laughable on its face to think that a country like the ones in Europe or in Norway or Switzerland aren’t doing enough to police forced labor.” And even if countries do enact and enforce the forced-labor import bans the U.S. wants, they would still need to prove that they’re enforcing them to Washington’s satisfaction before the tariffs would be removed, said lawyer Patrick Childress, a partner at Holland & Knight and a former U.S. trade official. “This suggests that no short-term path for countrywide relief from the new Section 301 tariffs will be available,” he said. Countries and industries reject the forced labor argument Many countries have pushed back against the Trump administration’s findings. Brazil, which faces a 12.5% forced-labor tariff, called the U.S. move “arbitrary and unjustified.” The U.S. “chose to manipulate an issue of great importance to human rights and the struggles of workers worldwide in order to accuse 59 countries and the European Union of unfair practices,” it said in a statement. Australia also questioned the justification for its 12.5% tariff. “We believe that amongst all of the countries in the world, Australia does take the issue of slavery, modern slavery, seriously, and will continue to do that,” Trade Minister Don Farrell told reporters in Adelaide. Carve-outs have riled some industries. The National Council of Textile Organizations (NCTO), which describes itself as the voice of the American textile industry, protested a mechanism that exempts the Section 301 tariffs for textile and apparel imports from Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia based on those countries’ imports of U.S. cotton and textiles. “No other industry has been more disadvantaged by forced labor than the U.S. textile industry, which employs 453,000 workers and has lost 41 plants over the past two plus years,” NCTO chief executive Kim Glas said in a statement. “We remain strongly concerned that USTR’s textile mechanism will harm the very domestic manufacturers the administration seeks to help.” US forced-labor bans don’t always work The U.S. has two major pieces of legislation related to forced-labor import bans. The Tariff Act of 1930 gave Customs and Border Protection the authority to seize shipments where forced labor was suspected and to block further imports. But it had a big carve-out: If there was “consumptive demand,” meaning there wasn’t sufficient supply to meet domestic demand, imports were allowed regardless of how they were produced. The Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act that took effect in 2016 eliminated that loophole. In 2021, the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act was passed. It blocks imports from China’s Xinjiang region unless businesses can prove the items were made without forced labor. But goods made with forced labor can still make it into the U.S. In 2015, an Associated Press investigation found that slave labor was used in the fishing industry in Southeast Asia. Selain itu, kata Jeje, Pemkab Bandung Barat melalui organisasi perangkat daerah (OPD) terkait juga menyiagakan armada distribusi air bersih. Hal itu terdiri tiga unit mobil tangki BPBD, dua unit dari Dinas Perumahan dan Permukiman, serta satu unit dari Dinas Pemadam Kebakaran untuk memenuhi kebutuhan masyarakat di wilayah terdampak. Langkah lainnya yakni membuka layanan darurat distribusi air bersih. column12: Listen to this article in summarized format That said, the monsoon performance in June indicated that this year’s El Nino is not to be trifled with. The rainfall deficit in June was nearly 40%, which resulted in a delay in the start of kharif sowing, and reservoir levels dipped below normal levels. Conditions have improved considerably in July, with rainfall near normal levels. As a result, the cumulative deficit, which is calculated since the start of the monsoon season, has reduced to 16% as of July 27. However, spatial distribution remains uneven, with more than 50% of the country by area receiving deficient rainfall. The revival in rainfall has also revived kharif sowing, which is now tracking marginally lower than last year. From a sowing perspective, rainfall activity in July and August is key, as most of the sowing is completed during this period. Past patterns show that if the rainfall deficit is 10% or higher, the average reduction in food grain production tends to be 6%. However, over the years, the linkage between monsoon outcomes and food grain production has been gradually reducing. Over the last 10 years, the correlation between the two has dropped to less than 60% (FY16 to FY25) from 85% over the previous 10-year period (FY06 to FY15). This reflects the rising share of area under irrigation, which currently stands at 60%. The rising reliance on irrigation makes reservoir levels essential. The pick-up in monsoon activity in July has also enabled reservoir levels to inch back towards normal levels. As the linkage between crop output and monsoon activity has changed over the years, a similar pattern is seen between agriculture GDP growth and monsoon activity. The composition of agriculture GDP has changed over the years, with allied sectors playing a key role. The share of crops in agriculture GDP has reduced to 54% from 64% 10 years ago, while there has been a corresponding increase in the share of allied sectors. This change in composition has reduced the sensitivity of agriculture growth to fluctuations in the monsoon. However, a dampening impact on agriculture GDP is still expected if the rainfall deficit is larger than 10%. The impact on overall GDP growth will be much lower due to the reducing share of agriculture GDP in overall GDP. The share has reduced to 15% from 24% 20 years ago. Despite the reducing share of agriculture in overall GDP, it remains a critically important sector from an employment perspective. The sector still accounts for more than 40% of total employment in the economy. Services, which contribute 56% of GDP, account for only 34% of total employment. The impact on the rural labour market could dampen rural demand post the harvest season. For inflation, the monsoon is a key variable given the large share of food in the CPI basket at nearly 40%. History shows that there have been normal monsoon years that have seen a surge in food inflation, such as FY23 to FY25. Conversely, there have been years with large rainfall deficits, such as FY15 and FY16 (12% and 14% deficit, respectively), which saw food inflation reduce drastically (from 12.1% in FY14 to 4.9% in FY16). This time around, some pick-up in food inflation is seen at 5.3% as of July 2026. However, the rise is moderate if one considers the fact that last year food inflation was negative during the same period. Moreover, the weather has been far more volatile this year, with an unprecedented heat wave and a weak start to the monsoon in June. Globally, conditions are also not very conducive, with a jump in global food prices due to the West Asia crisis. The latter has increased global fertiliser and freight transportation costs. A further rise in food inflation is likely, but there are certain mitigating factors, such as adequate food grain stocks and supply-side management by the government. For FY27, headline CPI inflation is expected to be higher at around 5%, reflecting the combined impact of fuel and food prices. (Gaura Sengupta is Chief Economist at IDFC FIRST Bank.) India is the world’s largest rice exporter, accounting for about 40% of global shipments and the biggest importer of vegetable oils such as palm oil, soyoil and sunflower oil. India’s monsoon rainfall deficit has narrowed to 16% from nearly 40% at the end of June, following widespread rains over the past few weeks, although some regions are still facing rainfall deficits of as much as 40%.
